Section 1 of 15

Does the Creator care about your body as much as your spirit?

Some people talk about spiritual life as though the body does not matter. Others treat health as if it were the highest purpose of life.

The Bible brings both into balance.

Your body is not an object to worship, but it is a gift to care for. The choices you make about food, rest, movement, substances, and stress can affect your ability to think clearly, serve others, and enjoy life.

Taking care of yourself is not selfish. It is one way of honoring the Creator.

Illness is not proof that you failed

Read John 9:1–3 ↗.

Jesus’ disciples saw a man who had been blind from birth. They assumed someone’s sin must have caused his condition. Jesus rejected their conclusion.

Sickness may result from many things:

  • Genetics
  • Infection
  • Injury
  • Environmental conditions
  • Limited access to healthy food or medical care
  • Another person’s actions
  • The general brokenness of the world
  • Personal choices

Sometimes several causes are involved. Sometimes we may never know why a condition developed.

Health principles matter, but they should never be used to shame someone with a disability, chronic illness, mental-health condition, or serious diagnosis.

A person’s health does not determine their spiritual value.

Your body belongs to the Creator

Read 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 ↗.

The Bible describes the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Your body belongs to the Creator twice: first because He made you, and second because Jesus gave His life to redeem you.

That gives your body dignity.

Caring for your body does not mean chasing a perfect appearance. Health is not measured by whether you look like someone on social media. Bodies differ in size, ability, age, and medical need.

The goal is faithful care, not comparison.

Ask:

“What choices will help my mind remain clear, my body function as well as possible, and my life become more useful to the Creator and others?”

The Creator’s original food plan

Read Genesis 1:29 ↗ and Genesis 2:9 ↗.

In the beginning, the Creator gave humanity plant foods: fruits, seeds, grains, and other foods growing from the earth.

A balanced plant-centered diet can include:

  • Vegetables
  • Fruits
  • Beans and lentils
  • Whole grains
  • Nuts and seeds
  • Other minimally processed foods

Modern health guidance also encourages whole, nutrient-dense foods and reducing heavily processed products containing large amounts of added sugar, sodium, and unhealthy fats. Current U.S. dietary guidance emphasizes eating real, nutrient-dense food. ↗

Not every product labeled “plant-based” is healthy. Candy, sugary drinks, and heavily processed snacks may come from plants, but they are not the same as whole foods.

Health grows from the overall pattern of what you eat—not from one special product.

What about eating meat?

After the flood, the Creator permitted humans to eat animals. Read Genesis 9:1–4 ↗.

However, the distinction between clean and unclean animals already existed before the flood. Read Genesis 7:1–2 ↗.

Leviticus 11 ↗ explains the distinction more fully.

Among land animals, those approved as food both chew the cud and have a divided hoof. In the water, approved creatures have both fins and scales. The chapter also identifies birds and other animals that were not to be eaten.

This means pork and shellfish are not included in the Creator’s approved food categories.

The distinction was not invented by a modern church or limited to one human culture. It appears in the Bible before Israel existed as a nation.

A vegetarian diet is not required for salvation. The Bible permits clean meat. However, many people choose to eat mostly or entirely plant-based foods for health, stewardship, or personal reasons.

Whatever you choose, avoid making food a reason for pride or judging people.

Didn’t the New Testament make every animal clean?

Read Acts 10:9–28 ↗.

Peter saw a vision involving a sheet filled with animals. A voice told him to rise, kill, and eat. Peter answered that he had never eaten anything common or unclean.

This happened years after Jesus returned to heaven. Peter still understood the distinction between clean and unclean animals.

The vision’s meaning became clear when Peter entered the home of Cornelius, a Gentile. Peter explained:

“God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean.”

The vision was about people—not a change in the Creator’s food instructions. God was teaching Peter that the gospel reaches every nation.

Read Mark 7:1–23 ↗.

This passage addresses ceremonial handwashing and the false idea that eating with unwashed hands spiritually contaminates a person. Jesus taught that evil comes from the heart. He was not reclassifying animals or changing the instructions of Leviticus 11 ↗.

Food and culture

Food can carry memories, family connections, and history. There is no single Native diet. Foods differ among nations, regions, seasons, and families.

You do not need to abandon every family recipe or adopt an expensive, unfamiliar menu to live healthfully.

Keep what is nourishing and consistent with the Bible. Adapt recipes when helpful. Use the foods available to you. If fresh produce is difficult to find or afford, frozen vegetables, frozen fruit, canned beans, oats, brown rice, and other simple foods may provide practical options.

Access matters. People should not be judged for choices shaped by income, location, transportation, or what nearby stores sell.

Begin with what you have and make the best next choice available.

Drink water regularly

Water supports nearly every system in the body.

Sugary drinks, energy drinks, and frequent high-caffeine beverages can add large amounts of sugar or stimulants while doing little to build long-term health.

Make water your regular drink when it is safe and available.

The amount you need varies with body size, weather, activity, pregnancy, illness, and medications. Certain heart or kidney conditions may require special fluid instructions, so follow the guidance of your medical professional.

A simple practice is to keep water nearby and drink throughout the day instead of waiting until you feel exhausted or intensely thirsty.

Move the body you have

Read 1 Timothy 4:8 ↗.

Physical exercise is not the highest purpose of life, but the Bible recognizes that it has value.

Movement does not require an expensive gym membership. It might include:

  • Walking
  • Running
  • Dancing
  • Swimming
  • Cycling
  • Strength exercises
  • Active work
  • Playing a sport
  • Hiking
  • Exercising from a chair
  • Physical therapy movements

Current U.S. guidance recommends that most adults work toward 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening activity on two days. It also emphasizes that some activity is better than none. See the current federal physical-activity guidance. ↗

If you have an injury, disability, chronic condition, or have been inactive for a long time, adapt movement to your abilities and ask a qualified professional for guidance.

Do not punish your body with exercise. Train it patiently.

Ten minutes today is better than a perfect plan you never begin.

Receive the gift of rest

Read Mark 6:31 ↗.

Jesus told His disciples:

“Come aside by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.”

Sleep is not laziness. Your body needs regular time to repair and restore itself.

Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep each day, although individual needs vary. The CDC provides sleep recommendations by age. ↗

Helpful practices may include:

  • Keeping a regular bedtime
  • Reducing caffeine late in the day
  • Dimming lights before bed
  • Moving your phone away from the bed
  • Making the room quiet and dark when possible
  • Avoiding heavy meals immediately before sleeping
  • Speaking with a health professional about ongoing insomnia, loud snoring, breathing pauses, or severe daytime sleepiness

The Creator also gave the seventh-day Sabbath as weekly rest. Daily sleep restores the body. Sabbath rest reminds the whole person that life does not depend entirely on constant labor.

Enjoy sunlight wisely

Sunlight helps regulate the body’s daily rhythm and supports important biological processes.

Spend reasonable time outside when weather and safety allow. Morning light may be especially helpful for establishing a consistent sleep-and-wake pattern.

At the same time, avoid sunburn and excessive ultraviolet exposure. Use shade, appropriate clothing, and skin protection when needed.

People differ in skin tone, health conditions, medications, and vitamin D needs. If you have concerns, ask a qualified medical professional rather than attempting to diagnose yourself.

The Creator’s gifts should be enjoyed with wisdom.

Breathe and make room for fresh air

The Creator formed humanity and breathed life into the first person. Read Genesis 2:7 ↗.

When possible, spend time where the air is clean. Open windows when conditions are safe, improve indoor ventilation, and avoid smoke-filled spaces.

Slow breathing can also help you pause during a stressful moment:

  1. Relax your shoulders.
  2. Breathe in slowly.
  3. Exhale without rushing.
  4. Bring your thoughts back to the Creator.

Breathing exercises do not solve every anxiety disorder or medical problem, but they can create a moment of calm in which to pray and choose your next step.

Practice temperance

Read 1 Corinthians 9:24–27 ↗.

Temperance means self-control through the power of the Holy Spirit.

It includes avoiding what is harmful and using what is good with wisdom.

This means staying free from:

  • Alcohol
  • Commercial tobacco and nicotine addiction
  • Recreational intoxicants
  • Misused prescription drugs
  • Other substances that impair judgment or damage health

It also means using good things in balanced ways.

Food, work, exercise, entertainment, and technology can become harmful when they control the mind or crowd out relationships, sleep, worship, and responsibility.

The question is not only:

“Is this allowed?”

Also ask:

“Is this helping me become clear-minded, free, and faithful?”

Care for your mental and emotional health

Read Psalm 42:5–11 ↗.

Faithful people can experience depression, anxiety, grief, trauma, and emotional exhaustion.

Prayer is important, but struggling emotionally does not mean you have failed to pray correctly. The Creator may work through counseling, medical care, healthy relationships, rest, support groups, and medication.

Talk to someone if you are:

  • Unable to function normally
  • Constantly overwhelmed
  • Having frequent panic attacks
  • Reliving traumatic experiences
  • Using substances to cope
  • Feeling that life is not worth living
  • Thinking about harming yourself or someone else

In the United States, call or text 988 ↗ for immediate support during a suicidal or emotional crisis. Call 911 when someone is in immediate danger.

You deserve help before the crisis becomes worse.

Healthy relationships are part of health

Read Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 ↗ and Proverbs 17:22 ↗.

Isolation affects the whole person. We need people who can listen, encourage, laugh, pray, and tell us the truth.

Healthy connection may include family, trusted friends, elders, mentors, a counselor, a recovery group, or a faith community.

Not every family relationship is safe. You are allowed to maintain boundaries with people who abuse, manipulate, or endanger you.

Community does not mean giving everyone unlimited access to your life. It means building safe, honest relationships in which people help one another grow.

Trust supports whole-person health

Read Proverbs 3:5–8 ↗ and Philippians 4:6–7 ↗.

Trust in the Creator does not guarantee that you will never become sick. It gives you Someone to hold on to when health changes.

Prayer can quiet fear, direct your decisions, and remind you that you are more than a diagnosis.

The Creator may heal immediately. He may work gradually through treatment. He may give strength to live faithfully with a condition that does not disappear.

Whatever happens, your life remains in His hands.

Medical care is not a lack of faith

Read Luke 5:31 ↗.

Jesus said that sick people need a physician.

Medical professionals are human and can make mistakes, so it is wise to ask questions and seek another opinion when appropriate. But refusing all medical care is not proof of spiritual faithfulness.

Responsible care may include:

  • Regular checkups
  • Dental care
  • Recommended screenings
  • Taking medication as directed
  • Mental-health treatment
  • Physical therapy
  • Nutrition counseling
  • Emergency care
  • Asking questions about benefits, risks, and alternatives

Tell your health professional about supplements, traditional medicines, over-the-counter products, and prescriptions you use. Some substances can interact in dangerous ways.

Choose providers who respect your dignity and listen to your concerns. Tribal and Urban Indian health programs may offer culturally responsive options in some areas.

Health is not salvation

Read Ephesians 2:8–10 ↗.

You are not saved by eating correctly, exercising, or avoiding harmful substances.

Salvation comes by grace through faith in Jesus.

Healthful living is a response to that grace. You care for your body because it belongs to the One who created and redeemed you.

A person with excellent habits still needs Jesus. A person with serious health problems is not loved any less.

Health principles should make us more grateful and useful—not proud.

Begin with one faithful change

Trying to change everything at once often leads to discouragement.

Choose one clear step:

  • Drink water instead of one sugary beverage
  • Add one serving of vegetables
  • Walk for ten minutes
  • Go to bed thirty minutes earlier
  • Schedule a medical appointment
  • Ask for help with depression or anxiety
  • Prepare food instead of buying fast food
  • Put your phone away during meals
  • Stop using one harmful substance with appropriate support

Small choices become patterns. Patterns become a way of life.

Ask the Creator to guide your next step rather than waiting for a perfect moment.

Think About It

  1. Do you view your body with gratitude, shame, frustration, or neglect?
  2. Which part of your health most needs attention right now?
  3. Have you ever judged someone—or yourself—as spiritually weak because of illness?
  4. Which foods from your family or community support health and agree with the Bible?
  5. Are sleep, stress, substances, or technology affecting your ability to think clearly?
  6. What one change could you begin this week?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 ↗.

Thank the Creator for three things your body allows you to do.

Day 2

Read Genesis 1:29 ↗ and Daniel 1:8–16 ↗.

Add one simple whole plant food to your meals today.

Day 3

Read Leviticus 11 ↗ and Acts 10:9–28 ↗.

Write down what these passages teach about food and what Peter says his vision meant.

Day 4

Read Mark 6:30–32 ↗.

Plan enough time for sleep and place your phone away from your bed.

Day 5

Read 1 Timothy 4:8 ↗.

Choose a form of movement suited to your ability. Begin with a realistic amount.

Day 6

Read Proverbs 3:5–8 ↗.

Bring one physical or mental-health concern to the Creator. If professional care is needed, take one step toward obtaining it.

Day 7

Read Isaiah 58:13–14 ↗.

Receive the Sabbath as a whole-person gift. Rest, worship, enjoy healthy food, spend time with safe people, and notice the Creator’s work around you.

At the end of the week, choose one healthy practice to continue.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, thank You for giving me life. Thank You for my body, even when it feels tired, limited, or unwell.

Forgive me for the times I have neglected my health, misused Your gifts, or measured my worth by my appearance.

Give me wisdom about food, movement, water, sunlight, rest, fresh air, self-control, and trust. Help me begin with changes I can continue.

Guide me toward qualified medical care when I need it. Protect me from shame, extreme promises, and advice that could cause harm.

Jesus, remind me that healthy living cannot earn salvation. I care for myself because You created me, redeemed me, and gave my life a purpose.

Holy Spirit, give me the strength to choose what supports life and freedom. Help my whole life—body, mind, relationships, and spirit—honor You. Amen.

Remember This

Your body is a gift from the Creator, not a measure of your worth.

Healthful living includes nourishing food, clean water, movement, sunlight, fresh air, rest, temperance, supportive relationships, and trust in God.

The Bible distinguishes between clean and unclean animals and points toward a plant-centered pattern of eating. It also calls us to remain free from intoxicants and other controlling substances.

Illness is not proof of spiritual failure, and medical care is not a lack of faith.

You are saved by the grace of Jesus—not by perfect health habits. Care for your body because you are already created, loved, and redeemed.
